sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Caloboletus calopus is a stout bolete with a 5–14 cm grey-white to olive-beige cap, slightly downy when young and smoother later. Its underside has fine yellow pores, normally never red, which turn blue on bruising. The thick stem is yellow at the top and red lower down, with a distinct pale raised network. Pale yellow to whitish flesh blues after cutting, sometimes gradually. The spore print is olive-brown.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: An ectomycorrhizal ground-dwelling woodland species, often with beech and oak and sometimes pine or spruce. It fruits mainly in summer and autumn. Reported soil preferences vary by region; habitat alone does not identify it.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: The also-toxic Satan's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas) usually has orange to red pores when mature, whereas C. calopus has yellow pores. Other boletes also have red stems or blue bruising; compare pore colour, stem reticulation and cut flesh together. Do not taste a specimen to decide: characteristic bitterness is not a safe test.

sections.title: Edibility and risk
sections.text: The German Mycological Society lists C. calopus for gastrointestinal poisoning. Its bitterness persists after cooking. ANSES reports collections confused with other boletes; this guide classifies it as toxic and discourages consumption.

traits: Grey-white to olive cap, slightly downy when young
Stem yellow above and red below, with a conspicuous pale network
Pale flesh bluing after cutting; olive-brown spore print
Woodland with broadleaves and sometimes conifers, summer-autumn
safetyNote: A toxic or at least inedible bolete: the DGfM associates it with digestive illness. Do not taste it to identify it and do not eat it. Seek medical or poison-centre advice after suspected ingestion.
